amendments.rule: An English particle or adverb that realizes a Greek **preverb** rides inside the compound verb's own unit and is never `added`, as a discontinuous realization under rule 15 where the ASV separates them: `ἐξῆλθεν` → *went forth*, `ἐξέβαλον` → *cast out*, `ἀνέβη` → *went up*, `ἐπεβίβασαν` → *set thereon* at LUK.19.35, `προσηργάσατο` → *hath made more* at LUK.19.16, `ἀπολάβωσιν` → *receive again* at LUK.6.34. The head is the English word glossing the **verbal root**, never the particle. The corpus is unanimous: 963 units across 141 chapters carry such a particle and every one of them is `aligned`, none `added`, and the head stands on the verb word in all but one class. This is scoped to a particle **no other source token stands to answer to**. Where an expressed preposition does answer to it — because the particle is part of that preposition's own English gloss, as *out* is of `ἐκ` → *out of* — the whole English prepositional expression is the preposition's, headed on the prepositional word, and the compound verb keeps only its verb word: `ἔξελθε ἐξ αὐτοῦ` → *come* and *out of*, `ἐξῆλθεν ἐξ αὐτοῦ` → *came* and *out of*, as `εἰσελθὼν εἰς` → *entered* and *into* and `ἀπῆλθεν ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ` → *departed* and *from* do. Rule 36 is what decides that and says it in terms: an English preposition governing a prepositional phrase realizes the Greek preposition and not the verb it depends on, even where English idiom makes the verb phrasal, and a preposition is left `unrepresented` only where English realizes it nowhere at all — so do not leave such a preposition a bare *of* while the verb takes the *out*. That arm is scoped to where the ASV writes **one** English particle for the two, and the count of English words the ASV wrote is what decides it, as rule 94 decides a compound unit by that same test. Where the ASV writes a particle for the preverb **in addition to** a complete prepositional expression, each token takes its own and the verb does not go bare: `Ἔξελθε … ἐκ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου` → *Come forth* and *out of the man* gives *forth* to the imperative and *out of* to `ἐκ`, as `τὴν ἐξ αὐτοῦ δύναμιν ἐξελθοῦσαν` → *the power proceeding from him had gone forth* gives *forth* to the participle and *proceeding from* to `ἐξ`. That the preverb and the preposition are the same morpheme is not the test and does not strand the extra word: this rule's own count forbids marking such a particle `added`, and rule 36 forbids handing it to a preposition whose English is already complete, so the verb is the only token left to take it. A **noncompositional prepositional phrase** standing in the same clause answers to the particle in the same way, and the single English word is that phrase's rather than the preverb's: `συνήχθησαν ἐπὶ τὸ αὐτό` → *were gathered together* gives *were gathered* to the verb and *together* to `ἐπί` + `αὐτό` as one `noncompositional` unit under rule 45, the intervening article standing `unrepresented` under rule 93, as MAT.22.34 and ACT.4.26 read it and as ACT.2.44 reads the same phrase where no compound verb competes. Where no such phrase stands, the preverb keeps the word in the ordinary way, which is why `συνηγμένοι` → *gathered together* and `συνήχθησαν` → *were gathered together* keep *together* inside the verb's own unit. A preverb whose sense the following preposition's gloss does **not** carry keeps this rule's ordinary treatment, which is why `ἀναβαίνων ἐκ τοῦ ὕδατος` → *coming up out of the water* gives *up* to the participle and *out of* to `ἐκ` in one clause, and why `ἐκβάλλει … εἰς` → *driveth … forth* and *into* does. Rule 94 decides only whether the preposition and the word it governs form one unit, and does not decide where the particle goes. Where the compound verb governs a bare dative or genitive that the ASV writes with an English preposition, that preposition realizes the case government and rides with the governed word under rules 21, 36 and 69, as MRK.14.65 has it and as ACT.4.1 `ἐπέστησαν αὐτοῖς` → *came* and *upon them* and ACT.4.3 `ἐπέβαλον … αὐτοῖς` → *laid* and *on them* do. The one exception is an idiom that leaves no English verb word to head on at all: `Ἆρον` → *away with him* at JHN.19.15 and `Αἶρε` → *away with* at LUK.23.18 head on *away*, because nothing else was written.
amendments.why: Rule 106's expressed-preposition arm says flatly that the compound verb 'keeps only its verb word', and its examples are all cases where the ASV wrote a single particle (`ἔξελθε ἐξ αὐτοῦ` → *come* / *out of*). MRK.5.8 `Ἔξελθε … ἐκ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου` → *Come forth … out of the man* and MRK.5.30 `τὴν ἐξ αὐτοῦ δύναμιν ἐξελθοῦσαν` → *proceeding from him had gone forth* are the case it did not consider: the ASV writes a preverb particle in addition to a complete prepositional gloss of the same morpheme, and the rule as written strands that particle. The result is forced by rule 106's own commitments rather than by new evidence — the corpus never marks such a particle `added` (963 units, none), and rule 36 forbids handing it to a preposition whose English is already complete, so only the verb is left to take it. The amendment is the narrowest wording that closes the gap: it scopes the existing arm to a single written particle, adopts rule 94's word-count test by name, and says in terms that morpheme identity is not the test. Returned as an amendment rather than a new rule because the over-broad sentence is inside rule 106 and a later reader would meet it there first. Everything else in the rule is reproduced unchanged.

conventions: The compound ἀρχισυνάγωγος is one unit taking the whole English phrase 'ruler of the synagogue', headed on 'ruler' (MRK.5.22 'rulers of the synagogue', 5.35, 5.36, 5.38). Both English nouns gloss an element of the compound, so rule 66's gloss-versus-generic-completion test does not decide it; 'ruler' is the element the word names and 'synagogue' the one that qualifies it, exactly as 'priest' is what ἀρχιερεύς names. The supplied 'of the' is a rule 7 helper inside that unit, no source token answering to it. At 5.35 the italicized 'house' is folded in as the completion of the elliptical genitive 'the ruler of the synagogue's', its English being incomplete without it. Do not read rule 104's prefix-family analogy as putting the head on the stem word here.

In εἰς τὸ πέραν (MRK.5.1, 5.21) the expressed preposition takes its own English word ('to', 'unto') and the substantivizing article takes the determiner 'the', leaving the adverb 'other side' headed on 'side' per rule 71. Rule 42's 'of the' on the article is a different token — the article of the governed noun, which at 5.1 is τῆς θαλάσσης and does take 'of the'. So an article standing before an improper preposition is not the article rule 42 speaks of, and rules 2 and 26 forbid absorbing an expressed εἰς or τό into the adverb's phrase.

report: Read all 43 verses end to end against the 66-lemma candidate table. No cross-verse split found, so patches is empty.

Preverb versus expressed preposition (5.2, 5.8, 5.10, 5.12, 5.13, 5.18, 5.21, 5.24, 5.30, 5.32, 5.33, 5.37, 5.39, 5.40, 5.42) divides on the count of English particles the ASV wrote, not on the Greek morpheme: 5.2 writes only 'out of' and gives it to ek, while 5.8 writes 'Come forth' and 'out of the man' and gives one to each. That difference is licensed by the English, not a split.

Article treatments are consistent. A substantival article before a participle keeps only the pronoun (5.14, 5.15, 5.16, 5.18, 5.32) or the single relativizer under rule 90 (5.14 to); a prepositional-modifier article keeps the relativizer (5.26, 5.40); an attributive article across an interposed genitive takes 'the' (5.30, rule 57); and 5.33 / 5.34 / 5.36 differ only because one governs an expressed noun, one is substantival and one stands before a name.

Rule 20's two arms are applied by availability rather than word order: the article takes the supplied possessive at 5.3, 5.23, 5.29 and 5.40 where no pronoun is free, and is unrepresented at 5.17, 5.19, 5.22, 5.27, 5.28, 5.30, 5.31, 5.34 and 5.35 where one is. 5.29 writes both arms in one verse.

The candidate table is blind to added units, so the eight italicized words were read separately. Added: 5.13 'in number', 5.15 'even', 5.23 'I pray thee', 5.38 'many'. Folded: 5.19 'how', 5.30 'proceeding', 5.35 'house', 5.43 'something'. Every fold completes a token whose English was still incomplete and every addition has a spent or absent licensor, so rule 103's test was applied uniformly and no split hides here.

All eight BSB disagreements are documented convention differences and none is a genuine error: 5.7 (second attributive article, rule 23), 5.19 and 5.29 (article displaced by a free genitive pronoun, rule 20), 5.20 and 5.26 to (no English determiner, rule 23), 5.25 en and 5.26 eis (preposition absorbed into an English predicate, rule 36), 5.37 ouk (redundant negative, rule 41, which that verse's own note already predicts will be reported). Nothing was changed to improve the aggregate.

MRK.5.8 and 5.30 are a case rule 106 did not consider: the ASV writes a preverb particle in addition to a complete prepositional gloss of the same morpheme. Rule 106's expressed-preposition arm as written would strand 'forth', while its own commitments forbid every other home for it, so I amended rule 106 in place rather than adding a cross-referencing rule.

Not promoted: the archisynagogos head reasoning (both English nouns gloss an element of the compound, so the head follows the element the word names). It generalises and rule 66's archiereus datum agrees, but I would want the corpus reading of architriklinos before binding later chapters, and that is not worth the evidence round. Recorded as a convention instead.
